candidates.summary: The set \(\WFF\) of well-formed formulas is the smallest set of strings satisfying the following formation rules: \begin{enumerate} \item Every propositional variable \(P\in\Prop\) belongs to \(\WFF\). \item If \(\varphi\in\WFF\), then \(\neg\varphi\in\WFF\). \item If \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\) and \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then \((\varphi\circ\psi)\in\WFF\). \item No string is a well-formed formula unless it is obtained by finitely many applications of the previous clauses. \

candidates.summary: Let \(S\) be a set of strings over the propositional alphabet. Suppose: \begin{enumerate}   \item \(\Prop\subseteq S\);   \item if \(\varphi\in S\), then \(\neg\varphi\in S\);   \item if \(\varphi,\psi\in S\) and         \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then         \((\varphi\circ\psi)\in S\). \end{enumerate} Then \[ \WFF\subseteq S. \]

A propositional equivalence law is a valid schema of the form \[ \varphi\equiv\psi, \] with \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\). Each instance of the schema says that the two formulas have the same truth value under every truth assignment.

Let \(\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\) and \(\varphi\in\WFF\). The formula \(\varphi\) is a logical consequence of \(\Gamma\), written \[ \Gamma\models\varphi, \] if every truth assignment satisfying \(\Gamma\) also satisfies \(\varphi\).

For all formulas \(\varphi,\psi,\chi\in\WFF\), the following logical equivalences hold.  Commutativity: \[ \varphi\land\psi\equiv\psi\land\varphi, \qquad \varphi\lor\psi\equiv\psi\lor\varphi. \]  Associativity: \[ (\varphi\land\psi)\land\chi \equiv \varphi\land(\psi\land\chi), \qquad (\varphi\lor\psi)\lor\chi \equiv \varphi\lor(\psi\lor\chi). \]  Idempotence: \[ \varphi\land\varphi\equiv\varphi, \qquad \varphi\lor\varphi\equiv\varphi. \]  Double negation: \[ \neg\neg\varphi\equiv\varphi. \]
Replacing logically equivalent formulas inside a formula context preserves logical equivalence: \[ \varphi\equiv\psi \Longrightarrow C[\varphi]\equiv C[\psi]. \]
